prompt.context: Our client, Tarrant Fixtures, is a low-intensity manufacturing company that produces display fixtures for retail clients. The company's financial performance has deteriorated in each of the last three years. Specifically, they are concerned with the company's falling Return on Investment (ROI).
prompt.question: The CEO has asked us to look into this problem. How can Tarrant Fixtures get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What types of products does the company sell?
clarifying_info.a: Two types: Custom displays (50% of sales) — produced only when an order is placed and payment is received. Standard displays (50% of sales) — manufactured to open standard sizes/types and stored in inventory (built-to-stock). 5 standardized products account for 80% of standardized-product sales; the number of standardized SKUs increased from 5 to 12 over the last 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: How has revenue changed over the last three years?
clarifying_info.a: Total revenues grew 25%, from $100M to $125M, equally across both product types.
Costs of production (COGS, labor, SG&A, etc.) have remained stable as a percentage of revenue at 80%.

clarifying_info.q: Has the company made any new capital investments?
clarifying_info.a: No. The company has no new investments in Property, Plant, & Equipment (CAPEX = $0).

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to working capital?
clarifying_info.a: Total Working Capital employed three years ago was $80M; today it is $130M. Inventory levels increased 200% (primarily finished goods), from $25M to $75M.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive and market context?
clarifying_info.a: The market has grown 25% in total over the past three years. The client has remained the industry market share leader and has maintained 25% market share. There are several players in the market but competitive dynamics have been stable.

exhibits.title: Three-Year Financial Summary
exhibits.shows: A table comparing Year 1 and Year 3 financial figures including Revenue, Cost of Production ($), Net Profit, and Cost of Production as a percentage of Revenue

framework: Define ROI: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed
Analyze the numerator: examine revenue growth, cost structure, and net profit trends
Analyze the denominator: break down Capital Employed into PP&E and Working Capital (Inventory, AR, AP, Cash)
Identify root cause of Capital Employed increase and quantify impact on ROI
Develop recommendations to reduce Capital Employed and improve ROI

questions.prompt: Define ROI and identify which component is driving its decline.
questions.guidance: Strong answer: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. Candidate must know this formula; without it the case cannot proceed. Should hypothesize that either profits have fallen OR capital employed has risen (or both).

questions.prompt: Calculate net profit for Year 1 and Year 3. Is falling profit the cause of declining ROI?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the 80% cost-of-revenue assumption to derive net profit in both years. Net profit grew 25% in absolute terms, matching revenue growth, so the profit margin is unchanged — profit is NOT the cause of the ROI decline.

steps: Net profit grew 25% in line with revenue; margin is stable at 20%
math.answer: Net profit increased from $20M to $25M; not the cause of ROI decline.

questions.prompt: Examine Capital Employed. What changed and by how much?
questions.guidance: PP&E is constant (no CAPEX). Total Working Capital rose from $80M to $130M — an increase of $50M. A line-by-line review shows that PP&E, AR, AP, and Cash are all stable; the entire $50M increase is attributable to inventory (from $25M to $75M, a 200% increase).

math.setup: Capital Employed = PP&E + Working Capital; ΔWorking Capital = Inventory increase
steps: Conclusion: 100% of Working Capital increase is from inventory
math.answer: Capital Employed increased by $50M entirely due to inventory build-up.

questions.prompt: Calculate ROI for Year 1 and Year 3 and quantify the decline.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the ROI formula with derived figures. Assumes Capital Employed ≈ Working Capital (no new PP&E). ROI fell substantially despite profit growth, confirming inventory is the driver.

math.setup: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed (using Working Capital as proxy)
math.answer: ROI fell from ~25% to ~19%, driven by the $50M inventory increase.

questions.prompt: What are the root causes of the inventory increase, and what should management do about it?
questions.guidance: Candidate should link the inventory build to the Standard product line expansion (SKUs grew from 5 to 12). Strong answers will generate multiple creative causes and actionable solutions.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential causes of the inventory increase, and what actions can management take to reduce it?

categories.name: Root Causes
ideas: Proliferation of standardized product SKUs from 5 to 12 — more SKUs require more safety stock across a wider range
Inaccurate demand forecasts leading to excess safety stock being held
Obsolete inventories of discontinued or outdated product lines sitting unsold
Built-to-stock model for Standard displays inherently creates inventory risk when demand projections miss

categories.name: Recommendations to Reduce Inventory
ideas: Write off or work down obsolete inventory (note: a write-off causes an immediate hit to profits, so management may be reluctant)
Improve demand forecasting accuracy to set more realistic safety stock levels
Rationalize the Standard product portfolio — reduce SKUs back to the top 5 products, which drive 80% of Standard-display sales
Implement tighter new-SKU approval criteria to prevent future product proliferation
Consider shifting some Standard products to a build-to-order model to reduce finished-goods exposure
Develop a cohesive S&OP (Sales & Operations Planning) process to align production with actual demand signals

categories.name: Future Safeguards
ideas: Set maximum SKU count policy with mandatory review for additions
Tie safety-stock levels to data-driven demand volatility metrics
Regular inventory aging reviews to catch obsolescence early

recommendation: Tarrant Fixtures' ROI has declined over the past three years not because of falling profits — absolute net profit grew 25% — but because Capital Employed increased by $50M due to a 200% build-up in finished-goods inventory.
The inventory increase is driven primarily by the expansion of the Standard product SKU count from 5 to 12, compounded by inaccurate demand forecasting and the accumulation of obsolete stock.

To restore ROI, the client should rationalize its Standard product portfolio back to the top 5 SKUs (which represent 80% of Standard-display revenue), write down or liquidate obsolete inventory, and improve demand forecasting and safety-stock discipline.
risks: Writing off obsolete inventory will cause an immediate reduction in reported profits, which management may resist; this trade-off must be communicated clearly.
Reducing the product portfolio could disappoint some retail clients that rely on the discontinued sizes/types; a managed transition plan is needed.
Demand forecasting improvements require investment in systems or processes and take time to deliver results.
next_steps: Conduct a full SKU-level inventory audit to identify obsolete and slow-moving items and size the write-off.
Model the ROI impact of rationalizing from 12 SKUs to 5 SKUs to build the business case for the CEO.
Engage the sales and operations teams to redesign the demand forecasting and safety-stock process.
Establish a product portfolio governance process to prevent renewed SKU proliferation.
